source_read: PDF, printed pp. 121–133 (all 13 pages; Tables 1–4, printed sideways, read on rotated renders at 150 dpi; Figure 1 checked on the render; Figure 2 marker positions read exactly from the page's vector drawing)

claims.overstatement: Two parts go beyond this source. (1) 'People who kept using frequently also improved ... on spatial working memory (errors 29.58 to 19.92), pattern recognition (83.68% to 89.04%)': for these two tasks the paper reports only main effects of group, with no test of change over time; the frequent group's only tested gains are strategy (P = 0.003) and Stockings (P = 0.003). Also, not all of the group 'kept using frequently': 22 of 25 were still using at least monthly, mean frequency fell from 20.08 to 16.0 days a month (range 1–28 at follow-up; not significant), and the gains on these two tasks went with reductions in amount (Fig. 2). (2) 'The 24 of them retested a year later': at follow-up 3 members of the abstinent group were again using ketamine regularly, at least monthly (Table 2), and the group's hair ketamine rose from 4.92 to 14.89 ng/mg, so not all of them were still abstinent; the text gives 24 retested but Tables 1 and 2 give 23.
claims.note: Numbers from this source check: Table 3 (p. 127) gives 29.58 to 19.92, 83.68% to 89.04%, Stockings 7.67 to 9.50; correlations printed r = 0.623 (P = 0.004) and r = -0.732 (P < 0.001) on p. 129. Editors' calculation reproduced: from the exact marker coordinates of Fig. 2 (p. 130) I get r = 0.553 (22 markers, P about 0.008) and r = -0.551 (25 markers, P about 0.004), i.e. about 0.55 and -0.55. Two further observations: the y-values of the 20 round markers in panel B are exactly the negatives of those in panel A, and panel A's mean change in errors is +12.2 while Table 3 shows the group's errors falling by 9.66, so panel A plots baseline minus follow-up on both axes (labels say 'change'); the double reversal leaves the directions as the authors state. The text says the correlations were run in the groups still using ketamine, while the heading and figure say the frequent group only. 'Letter fluency fell ... also in both control groups' is right on Table 3 means (polydrug 17.33 to 15.25, non-drug 16.32 to 14.53, as against frequent 16.38 to 13.48 and abstinent 17.36 to 15.12; infrequent rose 15.21 to 17.25), although only the frequent (P = 0.046) and abstinent (P = 0.023) declines were reported as significant. 'The only study that retested the same people after they cut down' is defensible only for a group defined by cutting down: this study also retested the same people and related each person's change in amount to change in scores, but too few changed their use for subgroup analyses (p. 130).

anchors.locator: Materials and methods › Participants and design, 3rd paragraph
anchors.extracted: 80% retested after a mean of 366.6 (92.11) days: 25 frequent, 27 infrequent, 24 abstinent, 23 polydrug, 20 non-drug (Tables 1 and 2 instead give 23 abstinent, 24 polydrug and 21 non-drug). Tests with two versions counterbalanced across sessions; the three CANTAB tasks (spatial working memory, pattern recognition, Stockings) had only one version.

Frequent: regular (at least monthly) use by 30 then 22; frequency 20.08 (7.41) then 16.0 (10.01) days a month, follow-up range 1–28; amount 2.77 (2.42) then 2.18 (1.82) g; days since last use 2 (2.60), range 1–14, then 35.44 (94.59), range 1–340. Ex-ketamine at follow-up (n = 23): 3 using regularly (at least monthly), 2.63 (5.91) days a month, days since last use 34.71 (50.49), range 0–140 (the text on p. 124 gives 540.54 (691.19) days for the same measure).

anchors.locator: Results › Ketamine use (Table 2), 1st paragraph; p. 126 Results › Hair analysis, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: No main effects of time or interactions for frequency or amount of ketamine use. Hair ketamine: frequent 295.90 then 241.50; infrequent 21.82 then 48.43; abstinent 4.92 then 14.89 ng/mg; polydrug controls 1.63 (6.34) at follow-up.

anchors.locator: Table 3 (all rows); p. 126 Results › Cognitive assessments, spatial working memory (errors, strategy), Stockings and pattern recognition paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Frequent group, initial then follow-up: SWM errors 29.58 then 19.92 (others 11.48–18.32 then 12.48–15.89); strategy 31.63 then 27.33 (within-group improvement P = 0.003 after interaction F(4,108) = 2.59, P = 0.041); Stockings 7.67 then 9.50 (P = 0.003 within the frequent group; interaction only a trend, F(4,108) = 2.14, P = 0.081; others 9.33–9.87 at follow-up); pattern recognition 83.68% then 89.04%. For errors and pattern recognition only group main effects are reported.
Authors attribute the frequent group's Stockings and strategy gains partly to practice (tasks with only one version) and to its poor baseline leaving more room to improve.

anchors.locator: Results › Correlations between change in amount of ketamine use and other measures in frequent users (Fig. 2), 1st paragraph; Fig. 2 (p. 130)
anchors.extracted: Change in self-reported amount over the year correlated positively with change in SWM errors (r = 0.623, P = 0.004) and negatively with change in pattern-recognition percentage correct (r = -0.732, P < 0.001); outliers over 3 SD removed and threshold P < 0.01 (p. 124). Reader's calculation from the plotted points: r = 0.553 (22 points) and -0.551 (25 points).

anchors.locator: Results › Fluency › Verbal fluency, 1st paragraph; Table 3 (p. 127)
anchors.extracted: Letter fluency: time x group F(4,108) = 2.84, P = 0.027; time F(1,108) = 6.83, P = 0.01; poorer at follow-up in the frequent (P = 0.046) and abstinent (P = 0.023) groups; table means also fall in the polydrug (17.33 to 15.25) and non-drug (16.32 to 14.53) groups, and rise in the infrequent group (15.21 to 17.25).

Abstinent group showed no cognitive deficits against the non-drug or polydrug groups at either session, and no improvement with longer abstinence; authors think it most plausible that the group had already recovered, but say 'these data cannot really speak to this issue'.

anchors.locator: Discussion › The profile of a ketamine user, 1st paragraph (with Methodological considerations, 1st paragraph, p. 131)
anchors.extracted: Abstinent group had not used as heavily as the frequent group, though some had used daily. Few participants changed their use over the year, and a year may have been too short to see recovery or progressive deficits.

claims.overstatement: 'The frequent group's scores averaged over both sessions were still lower on ... pattern recognition' overstates the comparison the claim is about: on pattern recognition the frequent group was lower than the infrequent and ex-ketamine groups (P < 0.01) but not significantly lower than the polydrug or non-drug controls; only spatial working-memory errors were higher than all other groups (P < 0.05). The authors' discussion (p. 129) generalises in the same way.
claims.note: Numbers check against Table 3 (p. 127) and Table 2 (p. 125): 25 of 30 frequent retested; errors 29.58 to 19.92 (others 11.48–18.32, then 12.48–15.89); pattern recognition 83.68% to 89.04% (controls 88.41% and 89.58% at follow-up); Stockings 7.67 to 9.50 (others 9.33–9.87); 22 of 25 still using at least monthly. 366.6 days is the mean retest interval for the whole sample, not the frequent group alone. Reporting problems: the SWM-errors group effect is printed F(4,108) = 4.16, P = 0.04, but that F gives P about 0.004, and the identical F and P are printed for the delusions inventory (p. 128), suggesting a copying error; the pattern-recognition F is printed with df (1,108) where a five-group effect has (4,108) (with 4,108 the printed P = 0.002 fits). For the same baseline session this paper gives the frequent group 2 (SD 2.60) days since last use, range 1–14, against 1.6 (1.27), range 1–7 in Morgan et al. (2009); the claim's 'one to seven days' follows the 2009 paper. The authors could not verify 24-hour abstinence biologically (p. 132). Of the 5 frequent participants not retested, 2 had died during the year in ketamine-related accidents (p. 132), so the retested group is a selected one.

Frequent 83.68 (10.27) then 89.04 (7.24) vs polydrug 90.53 then 88.41 and non-drug 90.79 then 89.58.

anchors.locator: Results › Stockings of Cambridge task paragraph (continues in right column); Table 3 (p. 127)
anchors.extracted: Time F(1,108) = 9.73, P = 0.002; group only a trend, F(4,108) = 2.30, P = 0.064; trend interaction F(4,108) = 2.14, P = 0.081 reflecting better follow-up performance in the frequent group (P = 0.003): 7.67 then 9.50 vs 9.33–9.87 in the others at follow-up.
Frequent group: 22 of 25 using regularly (at least monthly) at follow-up; frequency 20.08 then 16.0 days a month; initial days since last use 2 (2.60), range 1–14.

anchors.locator: Discussion › Methodological considerations, 1st paragraph (continues on p. 132)
anchors.extracted: 24-hour abstinence could not be verified with biological samples (ketamine stays in urine 1–2 days); testers judged none intoxicated. Frequent group differed in education and pre-morbid IQ (Table 1: 12.2 years and Spot the Word 46.25).

claims.overstatement: None in the claim. The abstract (p. 121) and discussion (p. 131) call the ordering of delusion means a dose–response effect that suggests 'a clear link with ketamine use per se', but the post-hoc tests separate the frequent group only from the polydrug and non-drug groups; the claim keeps to association.
claims.note: Values check against Table 4 (p. 128) and Fig. 1 (p. 129; y-axis is the number of yes responses, about 8.2 frequent vs about 3.95 non-drug averaged over sessions). Dissociation: frequent highest at both sessions (76.95 then 75.09; infrequent 66.00 then 66.92) but significantly above only the polydrug (P = 0.015) and non-drug (P = 0.009) groups. The delusions group effect is printed F(4,108) = 4.16, P = 0.04, identical to the SWM-errors result; that F gives P about 0.004. Cross-paper inconsistency: this paper's baseline depression score for the 25 retested frequent participants (7.08) is far below the 11.48 that Morgan et al. (2009) report for all 30 at the same session; both can hold only if the 5 not retested averaged about 33.5 (reader's calculation). Likewise the frequent group's baseline amount per session is 2.77 g here (Table 2, n = 30) against 3.80 g in the 2009 paper. The frequent group also reported more negative life events over the year, a confounder for the rise in depression.

anchors.locator: Results › LES, 1st paragraph; p. 131 Discussion › Psychological wellbeing, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Frequent group reported more negative life events over the 12 months (F(4,104) = 4.30, P = 0.003; vs infrequent P = 0.016, polydrug P = 0.013, non-drug P = 0.006). Authors link the frequent group's depression partly to dependence and chaotic lifestyles, and the abstinent group's rise possibly to a change in lifestyle.

Authors call the ordering of delusion scores (frequent, then infrequent and abstinent, then non-drug) a dose–response effect suggesting a link with ketamine use per se; schizotypy (O-LIFE) fell over the year in every group except the frequent group (interaction F(4,105) = 5.60, P < 0.001).

reporting_issues.note: The part about post hoc tests after non-significant omnibus tests is confirmed. The inference that the d' post hoc values 'cannot all be right' holds only if the printed P = 0.002 is Bonferroni-adjusted (as the Method states for main effects of group) or, if unadjusted, below about 0.0023. An unadjusted P of 0.0024-0.0025, printed as 0.002, gives t squared over 4 of about 2.40-2.42 on 108 df, which is compatible with F(4,108) = 2.42 (P = 0.053). Correction: say the values are inconsistent if the P values are Bonferroni-adjusted as stated, and only marginally compatible if they are not.
The text's 2.2 (2.81) and 11.03 (9.72) do resemble the table's baseline 2 (2.60) and 11.30 (9.36).
All examples checked on the rotated render, including 18-32 days (ex-ketamine cannabis, follow-up).
Confirmed; the reader's blind reading did not catch this.

The reader reached the same reading (panel A baseline minus follow-up on both axes), which preserves the directions stated in the text.

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-E high overall; exposure misclassification at follow-up (baseline labels kept), loss related plausibly to outcome, and unreproducible key statistics justify the domains as judged.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial. Two small precisions: in results_show, 'recognised fewer patterns than other groups' should read 'than the infrequent and ex-ketamine groups' (p. 126; no significant difference from either control group); and the frequent group's 'improving on both tasks' (SWM errors, pattern recognition) describes untested mean changes, since only group main effects are reported for these two.

missed: Untested changes (p. 126, Results › Cognitive assessments): for SWM errors and pattern recognition only main effects of group are reported, with no time or time x group result, so the frequent group's mean changes (29.58 to 19.92; 83.68% to 89.04%) are not shown to be reliable; the only tested within-group gains are strategy (P = 0.003) and Stockings (P = 0.003). The card's risk-of-bias reasoning recommends citing 'improvement' on all four; for the first two, 'mean change, not tested' would be more accurate.

Cross-paper: the same baseline session's days since last use for the frequent group is 2 (SD 2.60), range 1-14, here (Table 2, p. 125), against 1.6 (1.27), range 1-7, in Morgan et al. (2009, Table 2); RI 9 lists the amount, frequency SD, hair, DES and PDI differences but not this one, which bears on claims stating that the frequent group was tested 1 to 7 days after last use.
